subject: Geography
topic: Soils of India — alluvial, black/regur, red, laterite, desert, mountain soils
description: Six major soil types of India: alluvial (khadar/bhangar), black/regur (Deccan trap), red (ferric), laterite (leached), desert (arid), mountain soils — distribution, properties, crops. SSC CGL/IBPS PO/UPSC standard.

questions.stem: The most widespread and most fertile soil type in India, covering the Indo-Gangetic plains, is:

options.option_text: Alluvial soil — deposited by rivers; covers ~43% of India's total land area
Black/Regur soil — found in the Deccan trap region, not the northern plains
Red soil — found in Deccan plateau and peninsular India, not the northern plains
Laterite soil — found in high-rainfall Western Ghats, not the fertile northern plains

questions.explanation: ALLUVIAL SOIL: deposited by three major river systems — Ganga, Brahmaputra, Indus (and their tributaries). AREA: ~43% of India's total geographical area (~6.4 lakh sq km). STATES: Punjab, Haryana, UP, Bihar, West Bengal, Assam; also Rajasthan (Indus system), Gujarat (river deposits). FERTILITY: Very fertile; rich in potassium and lime; low in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus (which must be added). CROPS: Rice, wheat, sugarcane, jute, oilseeds — India's food bowl. TWO TYPES: (1) KHADAR: new alluvium (near river channels); lighter, more porous, renewed by floods annually — highly fertile. (2) BHANGAR: old alluvium (upland terraces, away from river); darker, more clayey, contains kankar (calcareous nodules) — less fertile than Khadar. EXAM NICHE: kankar nodules in bhangar are a discriminating detail. MEMORY: 'Khadar = khadi/rough = fresh/light; Bhangar = bhang (heavier, intoxicating) = heavy/old.' PYQ FREQUENCY: alluvial soil = most widespread + khadar/bhangar in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims Geography — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Black cotton soil (Regur), found in the Deccan Trap region, is suitable for cotton cultivation because:

options.option_text: It has high moisture-retention capacity — retains water due to its clay-rich composition
It is the richest in nitrogen among all Indian soils — cotton is a nitrogen-hungry crop
It is the lightest soil — cotton roots can easily penetrate its loose structure
It has an acidic pH of 5-6 — cotton thrives in mildly acidic soils unlike other crops

questions.explanation: BLACK COTTON SOIL (REGUR): formed from weathering of basalt (volcanic Deccan Trap rocks, ~65 million years old). STATES: Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana — the Deccan Trap region. KEY PROPERTY: HIGH MOISTURE RETENTION — contains MONTMORILLONITE clay minerals that swell when wet (retaining moisture) and shrink/crack when dry. CRACKS in summer = 'SELF-PLOUGHING' (crack soil mixes deeper layers with surface). These self-ploughing cracks are a distinctive feature. COTTON SUITABILITY: cotton needs sustained moisture between rain spells — black soil's high water retention provides this. CHEMICAL PROPERTIES: rich in calcium, magnesium, iron, potassium, aluminium; POOR in nitrogen, phosphorus, organic matter. pH: slightly alkaline to neutral (7-8), NOT acidic (option D wrong). CROPS: cotton, soybean, sorghum (jowar), wheat, sunflower. MEMORY: 'BLACK SOIL = BLACK COTTON = MOISTURE MAGNET.' PYQ FREQUENCY: black soil moisture retention + self-ploughing in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Red soil gets its characteristic red colour from:

options.option_text: Iron oxide (Fe₂O₃) — high iron content, oxidised to ferric oxide under good drainage conditions
Humus and organic matter — high decomposition rates produce the reddish pigments
Laterisation process — aluminium compounds give red colour under tropical conditions
Manganese compounds — high manganese content stains the soil red in forested areas

questions.explanation: RED SOIL: colour due to IRON OXIDE (Fe₂O₃ — ferric oxide) under well-drained conditions. When iron-rich rocks weather in the presence of oxygen → iron oxidises → red colour (rust). LOCATION: Deccan plateau (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Chota Nagpur Plateau). PROPERTIES: porous, friable (easily crumbled); poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus; good drainage; generally poor fertility. WHEN DOES RED BECOME YELLOW? In waterlogged/poorly-drained areas, iron remains in the FERROUS (Fe²⁺, iron(II)) form → yellow-brown colour. So: well-drained + oxidised = RED; waterlogged + reduced = YELLOW. CROPS: groundnut, cotton, wheat, rice (with irrigation and fertilisers). LATERITE vs RED: laterite also red/brown but formed by LEACHING (loss of silica + lime, leaving behind iron and aluminium oxides) — different process. MEMORY: 'RED SOIL = RUST = IRON OXIDE.' PYQ FREQUENCY: red soil = iron oxide in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC Geography — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Laterite soil, found in the Western Ghats and northeastern India, is characterised by:

options.option_text: Intense leaching — silica and lime removed by heavy rain, leaving iron and aluminium oxides
High calcium and magnesium content — formed by deposition of calcium-rich sediments
Excellent nitrogen retention — humus accumulates rapidly in the humid tropical climate
Neutral pH — laterite soils are neither acidic nor alkaline, making them universally fertile

questions.explanation: LATERITE SOIL: FORMATION: in HIGH RAINFALL tropical areas, heavy rain leaches (washes away) silica (SiO₂), lime (CaCO₃), and humus from the soil. What remains: oxides of IRON (haematite, Fe₂O₃) and ALUMINIUM (gibbsite, Al(OH)₃) → hardened 'brick-like' soil. LATERITE = from Latin 'later' = brick (hardens when dry). CHARACTERISTICS: (1) Very poor in nitrogen, potassium, lime, humus. (2) ACIDIC (leached bases → pH 4-6). (3) Can be hardened and cut into bricks for building (laterite blocks used in temples of Kerala, Angkor Wat). (4) Infertile for most crops without heavy fertilisation. STATES: Kerala, coastal Karnataka, Goa, parts of Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Meghalaya, Assam. CROPS: Tea, coffee, rubber, coconut, cashew — all adapted to acidic, well-drained laterite soils. OPTION B wrong: calcium and magnesium are leached OUT. OPTION C wrong: humus is leached, not retained. OPTION D wrong: laterite is ACIDIC. PYQ FREQUENCY: laterite characteristics in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The Indira Gandhi Canal (Rajasthan Canal) has transformed agricultural productivity in the Thar Desert primarily by addressing the key deficiency of arid/desert soils, which is:

options.option_text: Lack of moisture — desert soils are structurally fertile (phosphate-rich) but severely water-deficient
Lack of minerals — desert soils are mineral-poor and require extensive chemical fertilisation first
Excessive acidity — alkaline desert soils need to be acidified before crops can grow productively
Too much clay — the heavy clay in desert soils needs to be broken up before irrigation starts

questions.explanation: DESERT/ARID SOILS of Rajasthan (Thar Desert): PROPERTIES: sandy texture (low clay), very low humus, low moisture retention, HIGH SALINITY in some areas, high evaporation rate. CHEMICAL COMPOSITION: surprisingly rich in PHOSPHATES and POTASSIUM; some areas have mineral deposits. The PRIMARY deficiency is MOISTURE — not minerals. IRRIGATION EFFECT: Once water is provided (Indira Gandhi Canal = 649 km main canal from Harike Barrage on Beas/Sutlej), wheat, cotton, groundnut, mustard have been successfully grown. PROBLEM WITH OVER-IRRIGATION: waterlogging and soil salinity — irrigation brings salts to the surface → salinisation. This is a key environmental concern in the Rajasthan canal command area. OPTION C WRONG: desert soils are ALKALINE (pH 7-8.5), not acidic — high lime and calcium content. OPTION D WRONG: desert soils are SANDY, not heavy clay. UPSC ANGLE: desertification, Indira Gandhi Canal controversy, groundwater depletion in Rajasthan. PYQ FREQUENCY: desert soil properties + Rajasthan canal in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC GS-1 Geography — 1× per 2 years.

questions.stem: The process of PEDOGENESIS refers to soil formation. In arid regions of India, the soil-forming process differs from humid regions primarily because:

options.option_text: Low rainfall prevents leaching — calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) accumulates at depth forming 'kankar' or calcrete layers
High evaporation removes all minerals — arid soils are completely devoid of any nutrient content
Wind erosion prevents soil formation entirely — no permanent soil profile develops in the Thar
Intense heat causes complete oxidation — all organic compounds are destroyed, forming pure quartz sand

questions.explanation: PEDOGENESIS IN ARID vs HUMID REGIONS: HUMID REGIONS: high rainfall → LEACHING (minerals washed downward or out) → calcium, silica, lime depleted from upper layers → laterite/red soils. ARID REGIONS: low rainfall → NO LEACHING → calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) and other salts ACCUMULATE at depth → form KANKAR (calcareous nodule layers) or CALCRETE/CALICHE. KANKAR: hard carbonate concretions found in bhangar (old alluvium) and desert soils — impedes root growth, reduces drainage. UPICA SOIL CLASSIFICATION (USDA): Aridisols = arid region soils (India's desert soils). Entisols = young soils with minimal development (new alluvium). Ultisols = highly leached old tropical soils (some laterite regions). OPTION B wrong: arid soils DO have minerals (phosphates, potassium) — they are not completely nutrient-free. OPTION C wrong: while wind erosion is significant, a soil profile DOES develop (A, B, C horizons can be seen). UPSC ANGLE: soil degradation — India loses ~5,334 million tonnes of soil annually to erosion. National Bureau of Soil Survey (NBSS), ICAR — Nagpur. PYQ FREQUENCY: kankar/calcrete in arid soils in UPSC GS-1 Geography, state PSC — 1× per 2-3 years.

questions.stem: India's National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP) classifies Indian soils into 8 orders using the USDA taxonomy. Which order includes most of India's fertile Indo-Gangetic alluvial soils?

options.option_text: Inceptisols — young soils with some horizon development; includes much of the Gangetic alluvium
Vertisols — the black cotton/regur soils of the Deccan Trap, not the Gangetic alluvium
Aridisols — dry desert soils of Rajasthan; not applicable to the moist Gangetic plains
Alfisols — moderately leached red-yellow soils; found in drier peninsular India, not the northern plains

questions.explanation: USDA SOIL TAXONOMY — 8 ORDERS IN INDIA: (1) ENTISOLS: very young, minimal development (some alluvial, coastal, desert dune soils). (2) INCEPTISOLS: young soils with basic horizon development — INCLUDES MUCH OF THE GANGETIC ALLUVIUM (fertile Indo-Gangetic plains fall predominantly under Inceptisols and Entisols). (3) VERTISOLS: swelling clay soils = BLACK COTTON/REGUR (Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat). (4) ARIDISOLS: arid/desert soils (Rajasthan). (5) ALFISOLS: moderately leached, red-yellow soils (parts of AP, Karnataka, parts of peninsular India). (6) ULTISOLS: highly weathered, highly leached (some laterite soils). (7) OXISOLS: tropical, intensely weathered (rare in India, some NE). (8) MOLLISOLS: prairie/meadow soils (some Kashmir valley, high altitude meadows). EXAM NICHE: USDA soil taxonomy applied to India is an UPSC-level question — discriminates well. NBSS&LUP Nagpur is the nodal body for Indian soil survey. PYQ FREQUENCY: USDA soil orders in India in UPSC Prelims, state PSC Geography — 1× per 3-4 years.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the distinction between Khadar and Bhangar within India's alluvial soils?

options.option_text: Khadar is older alluvium forming high upland terraces
Khadar is newer alluvium, renewed by annual river floods
Khadar carries kankar nodules; Bhangar has none at all
Khadar is limited to peninsular deltas; Bhangar in north

questions.explanation: B is correct: Khadar is the newer, finer alluvium deposited in active flood plains and is replenished every monsoon, making it more fertile. Bhangar is the older alluvium lying above flood level on upland terraces. Option C reverses a classic PYQ trap — it is Bhangar that contains kankar (calcium carbonate concretions), not Khadar.

questions.stem: Mountain soils of the Himalayan foothills are naturally acidic and rich in humus. Which commercially important crop thrives specifically in these acidic, well-drained hill-slope conditions?

options.option_text: Wheat, which needs deep, well-aerated alkaline soils
Cotton, requiring moisture-retentive black-soil bases
Tea, well suited to acidic, humus-rich hill soils
Sugarcane, needing deep alluvial, moisture-rich ground

questions.explanation: C is correct: Tea requires a pH of 4.5–6.0, good drainage, and abundant organic matter — all characteristic of mountain soils in Assam, Darjeeling, and the Nilgiris. Wheat (Option A) prefers neutral to slightly alkaline alluvial soils, while cotton (Option B) is specifically adapted to black (Regur) soil's moisture retention.

questions.stem: Black (Regur) soils develop deep cracks in summer and swell shut during the monsoon — a behaviour called 'self-ploughing'. The clay mineral primarily responsible for this shrink-swell property is:

options.option_text: Kaolinite clay, found predominantly in red and laterite soils
Montmorillonite clay, which has exceptional shrink-swell capacity
Illite clay, responsible for only moderate water retention
Vermiculite clay, which mainly enhances soil aeration levels

questions.explanation: B is correct: Montmorillonite (smectite group) has a 2:1 lattice structure allowing water molecules to enter between crystal layers, causing massive expansion when wet and deep cracking on drying — the self-ploughing effect. Kaolinite (Option A), a 1:1 clay dominant in laterites, has negligible shrink-swell capacity and is the most common wrong answer here.

questions.stem: In the laterisation process that forms laterite soils, intense tropical rainfall causes selective leaching. Which pair of elements is LOST from the profile while iron and aluminium are left behind?

options.option_text: Silica and soluble bases like calcium and magnesium
Iron and aluminium, which migrate down and concentrate
Potassium and sodium, removed mainly by bacterial action
Carbon and nitrogen, volatilised by intense tropical heat

questions.explanation: A is correct: Laterisation involves leaching of silica and soluble bases (Ca, Mg, Na, K) by percolating rainwater, leaving behind sesquioxides of iron (Fe₂O₃) and aluminium (Al₂O₃) — hence the brick-red colour and low fertility. Option B is the classic reversal trap: iron and aluminium are NOT leached; they are the residual fraction that remains and concentrates.

questions.stem: Red soils of peninsular India appear yellow in waterlogged or moist lowland depressions rather than in well-drained upland positions. The reason for this colour shift is:

options.option_text: Ferric oxide in hydrated (limonite) form gives yellow tints
Higher clay content in depressions alters light absorption
Sulphur compounds from anaerobic decay mask iron pigments
Manganese leaches out, exposing pale subsoil horizons below

questions.explanation: A is correct: In well-drained positions, iron exists as anhydrous haematite (Fe₂O₃ — red). In waterlogged or poorly-drained conditions, iron is hydrated to limonite (Fe₂O₃·nH₂O — yellow/ochre). The same parent material produces different colours purely based on drainage and redox conditions. Options B and C describe secondary soil changes unrelated to the primary colour mechanism.

questions.stem: Soils locally known as 'Usar', 'Reh', or 'Kallar' across parts of Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, and Punjab are unfit for most crops. The pedogenic process that creates these soils is:

options.option_text: Podsolisation — leaching of iron and aluminium downward
Laterisation — silica removal leaving an iron-oxide crust
Gleisation — anaerobic iron reduction in permanently flooded zones
Salinisation by capillary rise of salts in high-evaporation zones

questions.explanation: D is correct: In arid and semi-arid IGP regions, intense evaporation draws groundwater upward by capillary action; dissolved salts (chlorides, sulphates, carbonates of Na and Ca) precipitate at or near the surface, forming a white efflorescence (Reh/Usar/Kallar). This raises pH above 8.5 and creates physiological drought for plants. Gleisation (Option C) is a waterlogging process producing blue-grey mottling — a common distractor but the wrong mechanism.

questions.stem: Peaty and marshy soils of Kuttanad in Kerala and the Sundarbans coast are paradoxically rich in organic matter yet stubbornly infertile for most crops. The PRIMARY pedological explanation for this paradox is:

options.option_text: Excess nitrogen fixation prevents mineralisation of organic matter
Extreme soil acidity below pH 3.5 precipitates all macro-nutrients
Anaerobic waterlogged conditions inhibit decomposition of raw humus
Saline tidal intrusion permanently inactivates soil micro-organisms

questions.explanation: C is correct: Permanent waterlogging creates anaerobic (oxygen-depleted) conditions that drastically slow microbial decomposition. Organic matter accumulates as undecomposed or partially decomposed peat rather than being mineralised into plant-available nutrients — hence high organic carbon but low fertility. Option D is a partial truth for coastal soils but is not the PRIMARY cause; saline intrusion is seasonal and reversible, whereas the anaerobic suppression of decomposition is structural and continuous.
